practiceQuestions.q: Who among the following Later Mughal emperors was given the title 'Shah-i-Bekhabar' (The Heedless King) by historian Khafi Khan?
practiceQuestions.sol: Bahadur Shah I (Muazzam) was given the title 'Shah-i-Bekhabar' by Khafi Khan because of his state of complete ignorance about state affairs and his reckless policy of granting titles and promotions without regard for merit. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India / Satish Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: The famous 'Jizya' tax, which had been reimposed by Aurangzeb in 1679, was finally abolished in 1719 by which Mughal emperor?
practiceQuestions.sol: Jizya was finally abolished by Muhammad Shah Rangeela in 1719 at the persistent urging of Raja Girdhar Bahadur, his influential minister. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India / Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: Who were known as the 'King Makers' in the history of the Later Mughals during the early 18th century?
opts: The Nizam-ul-Mulk and Chin Qilich Khan
The Sayyid Brothers (Hasan Ali Khan and Hussain Ali Khan)
Maharaja Jai Singh and Raja Ajit Singh
practiceQuestions.sol: The Sayyid Brothers, Abdullah Khan (Wazir) and Hussain Ali Khan (Mir Bakshi), wielded enormous power and earned the title of 'King Makers' because they placed and removed multiple emperors on the Mughal throne between 1713 and 1720. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: The autonomous state of Hyderabad was founded in 1724 by which of the following nobles?
practiceQuestions.sol: Chin Qilich Khan, holding the title Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah, founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty of Hyderabad in 1724 after defeating Mubariz Khan at the Battle of Shakarkhera. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: Which Persian ruler invaded India in 1739, plundered Delhi, and carried away the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond?
practiceQuestions.sol: Nadir Shah, the Shah of Iran, invaded India in 1739 during Muhammad Shah's reign. He defeated the Mughal army at the Battle of Karnal and subsequently plundered Delhi, taking away vast treasures including the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India / Satish Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: Who founded the independent kingdom of Awadh in 1722?
practiceQuestions.sol: Saadat Khan, titled Burhan-ul-Mulk, was appointed as the Governor of Awadh in 1722 and laid the foundation of a virtually independent regional state there. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: The Third Battle of Panipat was fought in which year between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Third Battle of Panipat took place on January 14, 1761, resulting in a crushing defeat of the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau by the Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Modern Indian History / Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: Who shifted the capital of Bengal from Dhaka to Murshidabad in 1704?
practiceQuestions.sol: Murshid Quli Khan, appointed as Diwan of Bengal by Aurangzeb and later made nazim, shifted the provincial capital from Dhaka to Murshidabad (named after himself) in 1704 to distance himself from imperial interference. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which Sikh leader established the Sikh rule in Punjab in the late 18th century and founded the Sikh Empire by uniting various misls?
practiceQuestions.sol: Maharaja Ranjit Singh, leader of the Sukerchakia misl, unified the various Sikh misls in Punjab and established a powerful sovereign Sikh Empire with Lahore as its capital. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Modern Indian History / Spectrum]

practiceQuestions.q: Who among the following was the last Mughal Emperor, deposed and exiled by the British after the Revolt of 1857?
practiceQuestions.sol: Bahadur Shah II, popularly known by his pen name Zafar, was the last Mughal Emperor. He was tried by the British and exiled to Rangoon (Myanmar) following the suppression of the 1857 revolt. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part III]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the primary structural defect in the Mughal Jagirdari system during the Later Mughal period that accelerated the empire's financial collapse?
opts: Complete abolition of the Mansabdari system by Aurangzeb's successors
Severe shortage of transferable revenue-yielding jagirs vis-à-vis the number of claimants (Jagirdari Crisis)
Immediate conversion of all jagirs into hereditary zamindaris
Total transfer of land revenue collection rights to European trading companies
practiceQuestions.sol: Satish Chandra conceptualized the 'Jagirdari Crisis' as a structural mismatch where the number of nobles seeking high-yielding jagirs far exceeded the available crown lands and assessed revenues (jama), creating intense infighting and financial bankruptcy. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the nature of regional states like Hyderabad, Awadh, and Bengal differ fundamentally from the Maratha confederacy?
opts: Regional states were carved out by rebellious peasants, whereas Marathas were appointed governors by the emperor.

Regional states were successor states that emerged from autonomous administrative provinces of the Mughal Empire, while Marathas fought an anti-imperial liberation struggle to carve out an independent expansionist domain.
Regional states completely rejected Islamic law, whereas Marathas maintained strict Sharia compliance.
There was no difference; both operated as direct administrative units under imperial Delhi.
practiceQuestions.sol: Historians classify regional powers into Successor States (Hyderabad, Awadh, Bengal) which were Mughal provinces breaking away due to central weakness, New States (Marathas, Sikhs, Jats) born out of resistance against Mughal centralism, and Independent Kingdoms (Mysore, Kerala, Rajput states). [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence / NCERT]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following best explains the socio-economic policy adopted by Murshid Quli Khan in Bengal?
opts: He abolished the Jagirdari system altogether and distributed lands directly to landless peasants.
He introduced the 'Mal-zamindari' system and relied on local zamindars and revenue farmers (ijaradars), while regularizing revenue collection and transferring jagirs to Orissa.
He banned all foreign European trade and closed down the English East India Company factories.
He converted all agricultural land into pasture land for cavalry maintenance.
practiceQuestions.sol: Murshid Quli Khan streamlined Bengal's revenue administration by introducing revenue farming (ijaradari) and strictly auditing accounts. To satisfy imperial claims from Delhi without losing local control, he converted many Bengal jagirs into khalisah (crown lands) and reassigned jagirs in Orissa. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the significance of the Farman issued by Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar in 1717 to the English East India Company?
opts: It granted the British complete sovereignty over the city of Delhi.
It granted them duty-free trade in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa in lieu of an annual payment of 3,000 rupees, along with the right to issue dastaks (passes).
It ordered the immediate expulsion of all French and Dutch merchants from India.
It abolished all zamindari taxes across the Mughal Empire for European entities.
practiceQuestions.sol: Farrukhsiyar's Farman of 1717 (often called the Magna Carta of the Company) granted extensive trading privileges to the English East India Company, including duty-free export-import in Bengal for 3,000 rupees per year and the abuse of 'dastaks' which severely undermined Bengal's regional revenues. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India / NCERT]

practiceQuestions.q: The political fragmentation of the 18th century in India is best characterized by which of the following processes?
opts: A complete transition from agrarian economy to an industrialized capitalist economy
Decentralization of political power where regional elites asserted independence while retaining ideological allegiance to the Mughal symbol of legitimacy.
Immediate unification of India under a pan-Indian secular republic
Re-establishment of centralized imperial rule under the vigorous leadership of Nadir Shah
practiceQuestions.sol: The 18th century was an era of political decentralization and the rise of regional polities. While central authority collapsed, regional rulers maintained the fiction of Mughal suzerainty because the Mughal emperor remained the fountainhead of political legitimacy. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did the invasions of Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali have catastrophic impacts on the Mughal Empire beyond mere financial plunder?
opts: They resulted in the permanent annexation of Delhi into the Persian and Afghan empires respectively.
They exposed the military bankruptcy of the empire, destroyed the economic life of Northern India, and permanently severed Punjab from Delhi's control.
They led to the total eradication of Islam in northern India and the rise of Buddhist kingdoms.
They forced the Mughal emperors to sign subsidiary alliances with European powers.
practiceQuestions.sol: The foreign invasions shattered Delhi's military prestige, drained its treasury, devastated the rich Gangetic plains trade, and detached Punjab as a constant battleground, leaving the Mughals powerless against internal rebels and European expansionists. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the revenue farming system (Ijaradari) introduced during the Later Mughal period impact the peasantry and agrarian economy?
opts: It protected peasants from high taxation and ensured sustainable agricultural growth.
It subjected peasants to extreme exploitation, over-taxation, and coercion by revenue contractors who sought maximum profit within short lease periods.
It eliminated middlemen entirely and established direct cooperative farming.
It led to the conversion of all food crop lands into export-oriented cotton plantations supervised by the state.
practiceQuestions.sol: Under the Ijaradari system, the state auctioned revenue collection rights to the highest bidder (revenue farmer). Since these contractors held short-term leases, they extracted maximum revenue through ruthless extortion, ruining peasants and ruining long-term agrarian stability. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the principal objective behind the establishment of autonomous states like Awadh and Hyderabad by their founders?
opts: To completely eradicate Mughal administrative traditions and replace them with British common law
To safeguard regional administrative stability, economic prosperity, and personal political ambitions amidst the anarchy at the imperial capital.
To launch a pan-Islamic crusade against the Maratha confederacy
To invite foreign European companies to take over the internal administration
practiceQuestions.sol: Founders like Nizam-ul-Mulk in Hyderabad and Saadat Khan in Awadh were pragmatic imperial nobles who realized the central court in Delhi was failing. They carved out autonomous states primarily to preserve administrative order, ensure revenue security, and protect their own political stature. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did the Maratha expansion into Northern India during the mid-18th century fail to establish a stable, centralized imperial substitute for the Mughals?
opts: They lacked military capability and were easily defeated by regional peasants.
Their expansionist methods relied heavily on predatory taxation (Chauth and Sardeshmukhi) rather than systemic administrative integration, which alienated local rulers and populations.
They signed a formal treaty with the British prohibiting any territorial governance outside Maharashtra.
They strictly converted to foreign religions, losing the support of Hindu chieftains.
practiceQuestions.sol: While the Marathas became the dominant military power replacing the Mughals in Northern India, their reliance on extracting Chauth and Sardeshmukhi without building constructive administrative structures alienated potential allies like Rajputs, Jats, and Rohillas, culminating in their isolation at Panipat in 1761. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the core structural weakness of the Later Mughal military apparatus that rendered it vulnerable to regional rebels and foreign invaders?
opts: Total absence of gunpowder weaponry and artillery units
A corrupt, unwieldy, and faction-ridden army dependent on cash-strapped mansabdars who failed to maintain their assigned troop quotas (zawar and sawar).
Strict prohibition against employing foreign mercenaries
Complete reliance on naval warfare rather than land cavalry
practiceQuestions.sol: The Later Mughal military suffered from institutional decay. Mansabdars frequently falsified troop numbers (dag and chehra systems collapsed), soldiers were unpaid and disloyal, and weaponry remained technologically stagnant compared to mobile Afghan and Persian forces. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the reign of Bahadur Shah I:
1. He adopted a conciliatory policy towards the Marathas, Rajputs, and Sikhs after Aurangzeb's death.
2. He granted 'Sardeshmukhi' to the Marathas but hesitated to grant 'Chauth' explicitly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Bahadur Shah I initiated a policy of compromise, releasing Shahu from captivity and reconciling with Rajput rulers (though control was loose) and negotiating with Guru Gobind Singh. Statement 2 is incorrect: He agreed to grant 'Sardeshmukhi' of the Deccan to the Marathas, but refused to grant 'Chauth' outright because of legal and imperial jurisdiction concerns. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India / Satish Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Sayyid Brothers (Hasan Ali Khan and Hussain Ali Khan):
1. They pursued a policy of religious tolerance and abolished Jizya during the reign of Farrukhsiyar.
2. They were ultimately overthrown through a conspiracy hatched by Nizam-ul-Mulk and Muhammad Shah.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The Sayyid Brothers relied on Hindu and Rajput support, abolishing Jizya and pilgrimage taxes to foster communal harmony. Statement 2 is incorrect (technically nuanced): While Muhammad Shah was involved, the elimination of the Sayyids was spearheaded by an anti-Sayyid faction of Turani and Iranian nobles led by Nizam-ul-Mulk and Muhammad Amin Khan, not Nizam-ul-Mulk and Muhammad Shah jointly at the initial conspiracy stage (Muhammad Shah was a puppet emperor manipulated by them until he broke free). Wait, let's look closer: Muhammad Shah was indeed the emperor, but Nizam-ul-Mulk and Muhammad Amin Khan engineered their downfall. Let's check correctness: Statement 2 is generally accepted as true in standard texts (Nizam-ul-Mulk and Muhammad Shah's faction). Let's re-verify: Statement 1 is definitely true. Let's make sure both are correct or 1 only. Actually, Muhammad Shah collaborated with Muhammad Amin Khan and Nizam-ul-Mulk to overthrow them. Thus both are correct. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements about the rise of autonomous Awadh:
1. Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk introduced a new revenue settlement that reduced the power of powerful recalcitrant zamindars.
2. Awadh under Safdar Jang and Shuja-ud-Daula witnessed an era of cultural synthesis, Urdu poetry growth, and administrative efficiency.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Saadat Khan curbed recalcitrant zamindars by implementing a revised revenue assessment and checking corruption. Subsequent nawabs like Safdar Jang fostered a composite culture, promoted administrative stability, and patronized arts and Urdu literature. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History / Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Nadir Shah's invasion of India in 1739:
1. The decisive battle resulting in Mughal defeat took place at Panipat.
2. Nadir Shah's invasion exposed the extreme military vulnerability of the Mughal Empire and resulted in the transfer of imperial treasures to Persia.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because the decisive battle was fought at Karnal (Battle of Karnal, Feb 1739), not Panipat. Statement 2 is correct: Nadir Shah crushed the Mughal army at Karnal, entered Delhi, plundered immense wealth (including the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor), and laid bare Mughal military paralysis. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements about the administrative features of Hyderabad under Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah:
1. He maintained cordial relations with the Marathas and systematically avoided all military conflicts with them.
2. He introduced administrative reforms, tolerated Hindus in high administrative positions, and suppressed local lawlessness.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect: Nizam-ul-Mulk did not avoid all conflicts; he engaged in strategic military contests with the Marathas (such as the Battle of Palkhed where he was defeated by Baji Rao I). Statement 2 is correct: He restored order, curbed corruption, reorganized revenue administration, and employed talented Hindu officials like Puran Chand in key posts. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Carnatic region and its Nawabs in the 18th century:
1. The Carnatic was originally a subah of the Mughal Deccan under the administrative control of the Nizam of Hyderabad.
2. The Nawabs of Carnatic (such as Dost Ali and Anwar-ud-din) eventually became practically independent of Hyderabad's control, facilitating European intervention.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. The Carnatic was legally a dependency of the Nizam's viceroyalty of the Deccan. However, Saadatullah Khan and his successors made the nawabship hereditary and autonomous of Hyderabad, creating political instability that the French and British exploited during the Carnatic Wars. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India / NCERT]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Sikh misls and Maharaja Ranjit Singh:
1. The Sikh confederacy (Dal Khalsa) was organized into twelve military units known as misls before Ranjit Singh unified them.
2. Maharaja Ranjit Singh abolished traditional Sikh religious laws and replaced them entirely with British common law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: In the 18th century, the Sikhs organized themselves into the Dal Khalsa, divided into 12 misls that controlled different regions of Punjab. Statement 2 is incorrect: Ranjit Singh governed based on traditional customs, Hindu-Sikh legal norms, and Sharia for Muslims, and never adopted British common law (his kingdom was independent until 1849). [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Modern Indian History / Spectrum]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the economic conditions in 18th-century India:
1. While the imperial capital of Delhi experienced severe economic disruption and political pillage, several regional capitals like Lucknow, Hyderabad, and Pune witnessed cultural and commercial growth.
2. India's overseas trade completely collapsed during the 18th century due to European naval blockades.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The decline of Delhi did not mean total economic ruin everywhere; regional centers flourished as nobles and artisans migrated to prosperous provincial capitals. Statement 2 is incorrect: India's overseas trade actually expanded through European shipping companies, even though indigenous merchants faced intense competition and political subordination. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra / Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Third Battle of Panipat (1761):
1. The battle was fought between the Maratha forces and the Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali.
2. The Marathas were joined by all major North Indian regional powers, including the Jats, Rajputs, and Awadh Nawabs, in a united front against the Afghans.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The Third Battle of Panipat (1761) pitted the Marathas against Ahmad Shah Abdali. Statement 2 is incorrect: Due to their aggressive past policies and extraction of Chauth, the Marathas were completely isolated and failed to secure active alliances with the Rajputs, Jats, or Awadh (Awadh actually supported Abdali). [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Modern Indian History / Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the evolution of administrative institutions in successor states like Bengal:
1. Murshid Quli Khan, Alivardi Khan, and Siraj-ud-daula maintained administrative continuity by retaining Hindu officials in critical revenue and financial departments.
2. The revenue administration in Bengal was entirely centralized under European company administrators from the very beginning of the 18th century.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Bengal's Nawabs relied heavily on talented Hindu administrators and bankers like Ray Durlabh, Jagat Seth, and Ram Narayan for financial administration. Statement 2 is incorrect: European companies did not control Bengal's revenue administration until after the Battle of Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), well into the second half of the 18th century. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History / Bipan Chandra]
